item.title: How to Build an MVP App: Core Features vs Full Build
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

When figuring out how to build an MVP app, the most important step is defining the smallest version of your product that you can launch to solve a real user problem. Founders and developers often face the temptation to pack every possible feature into the initial release. Building an application triggers the urge to pile on user management, complex dashboards, and multi-layered permissions before writing a production line of code. The lean startup methodology counters this by forcing a strict definition of actual utility.

Understanding the minimum viable product approach

An MVP focuses strictly on the core problem your users face daily while cutting out secondary features like dark mode or deep analytics for version one. This approach reduces initial infrastructure and maintenance costs significantly while speeding up the time it takes to get real user feedback in production.

- Focuses strictly on the core problem your users face daily.

- Cuts out secondary features like dark mode or deep analytics for version one.

- Reduces initial infrastructure and maintenance costs significantly.

- Speeds up the time it takes to get real user feedback in production.

Identifying the core value feature

Finding the single feature that drives user value requires looking past what people say they want and watching what they actually do. When software projects stall, it is often because engineers spend weeks optimizing components that do not move user metrics. Technical efficiency matters, but writing clean code for the wrong feature wastes months of development time.

In your MVP, identify that single bottleneck or core workflow and build only around it. If your app connects service providers to customers, the core feature is the direct booking action, not the profile customization screen or the in-app chat. Prioritizing this singular path allows small engineering teams to ship faster and validate market assumptions without burning through capital on unproven ideas.

Managing technical debt and infrastructure costs

Every shortcut taken during early development introduces technical debt, but an MVP requires deliberate shortcuts to survive. The key is separating dangerous architectural debt from acceptable implementation shortcuts. Hardcoding configuration variables for a week is fine, but building a database schema that cannot handle basic relational queries will break your app by month two.

When scaling up a product later, systematic code restructuring becomes necessary to handle modern demands. Founders managing early infrastructure should keep cloud bills low by using managed serverless functions or simple Postgres instances rather than over-provisioning Kubernetes clusters. Monitoring resource usage early prevents unexpected cloud provider bills from cutting your runway short.

FAQ

What is mvp in mobile app development?

An MVP is the earliest functional version of a mobile application that includes only the core features needed to solve a specific user problem and gather feedback.

How long does it take to build an app?

Most focused MVP mobile applications take between six to twelve weeks to design, build, and launch when the feature set is kept strictly minimal.

How do I choose which features to cut?

Ask whether the app fails to solve the primary user problem if the feature is removed. If the answer is no, cut it from the first release.

Sources

Originally published at sundarprakash.in/blog/how-to-build-an-mvp-app by Sundar Prakash P.

item.title: When you replace a library, you also take over everything it did
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

DPOLens is an open-source MCP server that gives AI assistants the text of privacy law. Its search runs on the CPU, so it needs no GPU.

The usual way to run an embedding model in Python is sentence-transformers. DPOLens doesn't use it: with PyTorch's CPU build it installs about 1 GB, against about 200 MB for ONNX Runtime, the tokenizers library and NumPy. So DPOLens calls the model through ONNX Runtime directly, and does the tokenising and pooling itself, in about forty lines.

Those forty lines did their job. What they didn't do was what the library does without being asked. When a new instance starts for the first time, it embeds every clause of the law it carries, and while load-testing the community version, I found that this was the heaviest thing DPOLens ever did. In a container limited to 1.5 CPUs, about what a small server offers, it took nearly 23 minutes and peaked at 3.4 GB.

Two fixes made it 5.1× faster with 65% less memory, and the vectors came out the same. If you've swapped sentence-transformers for raw ONNX Runtime to slim an image, you probably have both problems too.

The setup

DPOLens's meaning search uses multilingual-e5-small. A new instance embeds GDPR, the UAE's data protection law and a sample company policy: 1,350 clauses, from 19 to 512 tokens long, 63 in the middle. The vectors go into Postgres with pgvector, so this happens once, before the instance answers anything.

Every run below embedded those 1,350 clauses inside the published DPOLens 0.1.0 image, the release before the fixes, from a fresh copy of the same database, with 4 GB of memory and a Docker CPU limit: 1.5 CPUs, 2.5 (what the community version gives this step), or none, which on my laptop is 10 cores.

What the library was doing: sorting by length

A model reads a batch as one rectangle. Every string is padded to the longest in its batch, and the padding costs as much work as the text.

sentence-transformers sorts its inputs by length before it batches them, so each batch holds strings of about one length. My forty lines didn't. They embedded 64 clauses at a time in the order they're stored, so a 20-token paragraph next to a 512-token article was read as 512 tokens. I counted: the clauses hold 110,000 real tokens, and the model read 304,000. Almost two thirds of its work was padding.

Padding costs memory too, and more than its share: the memory for attention grows with the number of strings in a batch times the square of the longest. A batch of 64 strings at 512 tokens was the heaviest shape 0.1.0 could make, and in stored order, every batch with one long article had that shape. Sorting alone doesn't prevent it, since the library still batches by count, so the fix also caps each batch by that measure, in the spirit of --max-batch-tokens in Hugging Face's Text Embeddings Inference:

# How much one batch may hold, as its clauses times the square of the longest,

# which is how the memory for attention grows: 64 clauses of 64 tokens, 16 of

# 128, or one of 512.

BATCH_BUDGET = 64 * 64 * 64

def batches(tokens: Sequence[int]) -> list[list[int]]:

found: list[list[int]] = []

batch: list[int] = []

for at in sorted(range(len(tokens)), key=lambda position: tokens[position]):

# Sorted, so this string is the longest the batch would hold.

if batch and (len(batch) + 1) * tokens[at] ** 2 > BATCH_BUDGET:

found.append(batch)

batch = []

batch.append(at)

if batch:

found.append(batch)

return found

Sorted and capped, the model reads 114,000 tokens instead of 304,000, and the longest clauses go one at a time. Budgets from half this one to eight times it were no better.

What nobody was doing: reading the CPU limit

The second problem isn't the library's.

Inside a container limited to 2.5 CPUs on a 10-core machine, Python's os.cpu_count() says 10, and ONNX Runtime, left to choose, starts a thread for each of them. A Docker CPU limit isn't a set of cores but a share of time, so ten threads took turns on two and a half CPUs' worth of it.

dpolens index build now reads the limit from /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max and rounds it up, so 2.5 CPUs get three threads. With no limit, it takes os.process_cpu_count(), which follows CPU affinity but not a time limit. Picking a fixed number doesn't work: three threads were the best with 2.5 CPUs, and with no limit they took 143 seconds, slower than 0.1.0's 129 with all ten.

The results

With 2.5 CPUs, each fix on its own, then both:

The two sorted rows in the middle used a budget four times the one that shipped. Threads changed the time and nothing else. Sorting changed both.

Then 0.2.0, which shipped both, against 0.1.0 at each limit:

The gain is largest where the machine is smallest, which is where a 23-minute first start gets noticed. The peak after, 1,213 MiB at every limit, is exactly what loading the model takes before embedding anything: embedding the whole law now adds nothing measurable to it.

Same vectors, same search

Padding is masked, so in theory it changes nothing. I checked anyway. 885 of the 1,350 vectors were bit-identical to 0.1.0's, and the rest differed by at most 0.00000011 in any component, the rounding of a batch with a different shape. Every published evaluation set scored the same recall@5, recall@10 and MRR, and a test now checks that each clause's stored vector is the one it gets embedded alone.

One more: memory that wasn't given back

Measuring the first start also caught DPOLens's worker, which embeds an organisation's policies, loading its own copy of the model for jobs with nothing left to embed, and keeping it. Closing the model wasn't enough either: glibc keeps freed memory for the process, so a process that held 875 MiB with the model loaded still held 440 after closing it, and 93 after malloc_trim(0). The worker now loads the model only when there's work, and gives the memory back after. It doesn't change what an instance needs, but it frees about 900 MB between jobs.

What I took from it

- A library is more than its API. Forty lines replaced sentence-transformers and kept the image about 800 MB smaller, and they also dropped the sorting the library does without saying so.

- Sort before you batch, then cap by shape. A batch's memory grows with its strings times the square of the longest, so that's what to limit.

-

A container's CPU limit isn't its core count. os.cpu_count() and ONNX Runtime both see the whole machine. Read /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max, and don't hard-code a number instead.

- Check the vectors, not only the clock. The same search results are the only reason the change could ship.

Everything here was measured on one laptop, with one model, over clauses whose lengths vary a lot: text of one length would gain little from sorting, and your seconds will differ. The batching is in index.py, the thread count in encode.py, and every measurement, including the options I didn't take, in #68. Both fixes shipped in DPOLens 0.2.0. To run an instance yourself, start with Get started. DPOLens is open source, under the Apache License 2.0.

First published on dpolens.com. DPOLens is an open-source MCP server that gives AI assistants privacy law and an organisation's own policies, clause by clause: github.com/alkhatibdev/dpolens.

item.title: Startup sues Apple in India over tap-to-share contacts feature
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Apple is being sued in India by a U.S.-based startup that alleges the iPhone maker’s NameDrop feature, which lets users share contact information by bringing devices close together, infringes its patented technology.

GG Technologies, the startup behind StayTouch, an app that lets users exchange contact details by bringing their phones close together, is seeking ₹15 billion (about $161.86 million) in damages and an injunction against Apple, per court documents reviewed by TechCrunch.

Santa Monica-headquartered GG Technologies filed the lawsuit in India in October after mediation proceedings initiated in April failed in September, the startup told TechCrunch. Pre-institution mediation is generally required before filing commercial lawsuits in India. The company also sued Apple in the U.S. in April over related patent infringement claims.

In its 781-page court filing in the Bombay High Court, GG Technologies alleged that Apple’s NameDrop infringes its Indian patent on technology that helps phones exchange contact details with nearby devices without requiring manual pairing. The company launched StayTouch in 2019, the same year it first sought patent protection for the technology in the U.S. It filed its Indian patent application in 2021 and received the patent in July 2024.

Apple introduced NameDrop as part of iOS 17 in June 2023. The feature debuted on iPhones later that year, with support for compatible Apple Watches arriving in October through watchOS 10.1.

“We are seeking an injunction to restrict the usage of the NameDrop feature which is native to iOS,” GG Technologies told TechCrunch. GG Technologies urged the court in its filing to restrict Apple from selling or importing iPhones and Apple Watches preloaded with NameDrop in India. The case has yet to be listed for a hearing.

In the U.S., the International Trade Commission opened an investigation into Apple’s alleged patent infringement in August, following a complaint from GG Technologies. The startup is seeking an order that could block imports of infringing Apple devices into the country, along with restrictions on their sale.

Founded in 2018 by Gaurav Goel, a graduate of the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Delhi and a former Goldman Sachs investment banker, GG Technologies developed StayTouch as an alternative to exchanging business cards. The app is available on iOS and Android.

Apple did not respond to a request for comment.

India has become increasingly important to Apple, both as a fast-growing consumer market and a major manufacturing hub outside China. The Cupertino company has expanded its retail presence in the South Asian nation, where iPhones still account for less than 10% of smartphone shipments, giving considerable room for growth.

Source: TechCrunch | Published: 2026-11-21 04:00 UTC

Original link: https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/20/startup-sues-apple-in-india-over-tap-to-share-contacts-feature/
